paragraphs: I came home in late October with one suitcase and a fairly [[humble]] plan: to help my mother for a season and then leave again. The [[previous]] autumn I had been a research assistant in a big city, and I had told everyone that small towns had nothing to offer. The bus dropped me two streets from the [[clinic]], and the rain had already [[upset]] my timetable. A delay was [[inevitable]] on that road, so I had learned to stay [[flexible]]. My mother's [[primary]] concern, as always, was not the rain but the queue of patients outside her door.

Her [[instrument]]s were old but clean, and she kept them in a case that had belonged to her own teacher. A thin woman in a [[stiff]] coat sat by the window, her face full of [[wrinkle]]s that the grey light made deeper. My mother [[prescribed|prescribe]] a small [[dose]] of a cheap drug and then explained, in a [[compassionate]] voice, why the fever would pass. She never [[exaggerate]]d a [[diagnosis]], and she never let a frightened farmer feel [[inferior]]. That evening, [[exhaust]]ed, she fell asleep in her chair with her glasses still on.

Two days later a boy came in with a cough that would not stop, and by then something had begun to [[infect]] half the village. The [[initial]] results were [[ambiguous]], and the technician's [[terminology]] meant nothing to the family. My mother had to [[undergo]] a long argument with the county hospital before they sent a second team. The drug would [[alleviate]] the fever but not the cause, and I tried to [[concentrate]] on the numbers while she talked to the mother. An old doctor from the health [[bureau]] arrived to [[instruct]] us in the [[preliminary]] steps. He said the water was the most [[plausible]] source, though he could not [[confirm]] it yet.

The family's insurer refused to pay, citing a [[clause]] on page nine. The wording was [[ambiguous]], and the [[representative]] on the phone read it in a tone that made us sound like [[alien]] intruders. Their [[advisory]] letter said the policy was [[conditional]] on a report we did not have, and that we should [[comply]] with a form that had never been sent. My mother asked whether the refusal was [[relevant]] to the boy's treatment; the woman said it was policy. In law, my mother told me, a rule that cannot be explained to a patient is not [[equivalent]] to justice. No family should [[deserve]] to be treated as a file number, and no clinic should [[assume]] that a small claim will be dropped.

We drove to the county seat to see Wei, a lawyer who had once worked [[undercover]] in a drug company. He could [[anticipate]] every argument the insurer would make, but he was [[reluctant]] to promise a [[client]] with no money anything. He said he could not [[prosecute]] on this evidence, though he could [[allege]] a pattern of delay; a [[conviction]] was rare, and an [[appeal]] was cheaper than a trial and far more likely to [[expedite]] a payment. He also said the director could not be [[arrest]]ed over a civil [[dispute]], however dishonest his letters were. Then he showed us a [[duplicate]] of a 1998 [[statute]] with a clause about rural clinics that almost nobody used, and after one afternoon of [[deliberation]] he took the case for a fee that was almost [[dirt-cheap]].

The town had been built around a mine, and its [[ethos]] still belonged to another century. In the assembly hall a [[portrait]] of a [[monarch]] hung above the door, and beside it a photograph of a [[sovereign]] who had never visited. The town had a [[democracy]] of sorts, but the mine owner's word carried more [[prestige]] than any vote. Owning land here was a [[privilege]] that came with an unwritten [[commitment]]: you did not sell to strangers. My grandfather used to say that a [[statute]] on paper and a custom in the square were two different animals. He also said that a bad decision, once made in public, is very hard to [[overturn]].

I spent three afternoons in the [[archive]] behind the library, a [[repository]] of maps, letters and ledgers. The [[format]] of the old registers was beautiful and useless, every entry written in a different hand. I tried to [[track]] each plot through ninety years of sales with [[rigorous]] notes, and I drew an [[approximate]] map of the old mine. Some chains were [[traceable]], others vanished into a [[rough]] notebook, and one file held the [[autobiography]] of a mine engineer written in [[terminology]] and silence. The paper was [[authentic]]; it held an [[outline]] of a 1958 town plan, the most [[concrete]] thing in the place, and its pencil marks were still [[discernible]] after sixty years.

On Thursdays I taught the science club at the middle school, mostly because my mother had volunteered me. We started with an [[integer]] and ended with the [[infinite]], a strange distance to cross in forty minutes. The children wrote their [[hypotheses]] on the board, and I asked them to [[articulate]] what they expected to see; one girl insisted the [[geo-centric]] model was obviously wrong, and she was right, though not for the reason she gave. We built a [[compound]] from two [[component]]s and watched a [[catalyst]] turn a cloudy liquid clear, a small [[phenomenon]] more convincing than any lecture. The [[atmosphere]] in the room changed at once, and my mother joked that my [[lingual]] skills were better than my medical ones, since I could explain a word but not a lung.

A travelling [[troupe]] came to the hall in November with a play about a miner's widow. The actress could [[portray]] grief without a single false note, and her voice was [[mournful]] and [[exquisitely]] controlled. The play was a [[tribute]] to the people who had stayed, and the audience [[appreciate|appreciate]]d it more than any [[display]] of fireworks. My mother [[commend]]ed the young actor afterwards, and his [[reputation]] in the town was made that night. She said the theatre did not [[entitle]] anyone to a living, but it did keep a place honest.

In December a [[multinational]] firm wrote offering to buy the mine and the land around it. Its [[annual]] [[revenue]] was larger than the town's whole budget, and its [[subscription]] to the local paper had bought it friendly headlines for years. The firm was [[upfront]] about one thing: it wanted the water rights, and it would pay for them. They offered a [[mortgage]] deal so generous that it looked almost [[implausible]]; a [[predecessor]] of the present manager had made the same offer and then [[retreat]]ed when the price of coal fell. This time the company was patient and [[promising]], and it had already begun to [[extend]] its [[possession]]s along the river. Villagers were told the offer would [[diminish]] after March, a claim that sounded like a threat dressed as a favour.

The assembly hall was full on a cold Tuesday, and someone put a [[motion]] on the table. After two hours of [[dispute]] the room reached a [[consensus]] that surprised everyone, though the company's lawyer made one [[concession]] after another, and each [[compromise]] cost the town something it could not name. There was real [[discontent]] in the back rows, and a young man tried to [[disrupt]] the vote. By nine o'clock there was a [[discernible]] change in the room and the chairman had to [[command]] silence; the [[intervention]] of two old miners did more than any threat. The motion passed by a narrow margin, nobody applauded, and the result [[frustrate|frustrate]]d almost everyone, which is usually the sign of a real compromise.

For a week I could not sleep, and I began to [[speculate]] about what I would do if the clinic closed. The [[potential]] loss frightened me more than the company did, and I [[resent]]ed the town for making me choose before I [[condemn]]ed myself for resenting it. My mother, who had every reason to be [[arrogant]] about thirty years of service, stayed [[humble]] and [[loyal]] to her patients. Her [[conscience]] was a [[constant]] [[companion]] that never let her [[retreat]] into easy cynicism, and she said a [[commitment]] made in public has to be kept in private. For the first time I understood that a place can [[determine]] a life without ever asking permission.

In January the mine's owners began to [[exploit]] the confusion, [[assert]]ing that the clinic was [[irregular]] and that its records were incomplete. A firm of auditors arrived to [[confine]] the staff to one room and to [[inventory]] every bottle on the shelves. They found nothing that could [[devastate]] us, though a single missing page was enough for a headline. The company's [[external]] advisers called my mother an amateur, a claim so [[implausible]] that even the editor laughed. Their [[intelligence]] on our case was poor; they had assumed that a rural clinic would never find a lawyer. In the end they took the [[extreme]] step of asking the county to [[overrule]] our lease, and the county refused.

In February the insurer paid, quietly, without a [[tribute]] or an apology. Wei said we could [[conclude]] the case there, and that a second appeal would only waste the family's money. The boy recovered, and his mother brought a basket of eggs to the clinic. I began to [[contemplate]] staying for another year. It was a decision that demanded [[deliberation]], and for once I did not [[associate]] it with failure. I had been [[preoccupied|preoccupy]] with my own career; now the town occupied me.

The school asked me to stay until the [[eclipse]] in March, when the science club would watch the moon cover the sun. I said yes, mostly because the [[tougher]] questions came from the children, not from the company. We built a [[frame]] of cardboard and a lens, and the whole class fell silent at the first bite of shadow. The head teacher, who had once been a [[counselor]] and still spelled the word [[counsellor]] on the old sign, said my [[engagement]] with the children mattered more than my degree. She also [[overrule|overrule]]d my plan to cancel the trip when the bus broke down. A [[domestic]] quarrel over seats lasted ten minutes and then dissolved into laughter.

That night she said home has a [[connotation]] she could not explain, and that an [[authentic]] life is usually a small one. I told her I wanted to [[consolidate]] what I had learned before going back to the city, and we agreed to stay in [[contact]] with the lawyer, the school and the boy's family. I would [[associate]] that winter with antiseptic, wet wool and a [[frequent]] bus leaving at six. Nothing had been solved completely, but the town and I had begun to [[collaborate]] on something modest and real. Every building on the street had to [[conform]] to the same grey rules, yet the people inside were anything but identical.
